newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan considers partial cabinet reshuffle - TV.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan considers partial cabinet reshuffle - TV.

text.p: Taiwan is considering a partial cabinet reshuffle in an effort to counter popular disenchantment with the government over mounting crime, state television said on Tuesday.
Premier Lien Chan would announce the cabinet changes in the near term, according to the report, which quoted unidentified high-ranking officials.

Interior Minister Lin Feng-cheng, under pressure for public anger over a jump in violent crime on the island, would step down and be replaced by charismatic Ma Ying-jeou, currently a minister without portfolio, the report said.
It said government spokesman Su Chi would be replaced by vice foreign minister Chen Chien-jen.

Council of Agriculture Chairman Tjiu Mau-ying would also step down but the television did not name Tjiu's replacement. Some agriculture department have been criticised following an outbreak of a hog epidemic on the island which hurt exports.
A newspaper poll, released on Tuesday, showed Premier Lien Chan's approval rating has sunk to a new low.
Only 24 percent of 762 people interviewed by the United Daily News on Monday said they were satisfied with Lien's performance, down six percentage points from a similar poll a week ago.

Taiwanese were shocked by last week's discovery of the body of 17-year-old Pai Hsien-yen, daughter of actress Pai Ping-ping. Her kidnappers, who dumped her naked body in a river, have not been caught.
Results from another opinion poll, released by the pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party on Tuesday, showed that 46.8 percent of 1,429 Taiwan residents thought that Lien should step down.
It said 75.7 percent of respondents thought Taiwan's social order was deteriorating rapidly.
More than 50,000 people demonstrated on Sunday to demand the resignation of Lien and a cabinet reshuffle.
About 40 Taiwan students rallied in front of the island's cabinet building on Monday to protest the worsening crime levels and ask Lien to take responsibility for the situation.
President Lee Teng-hui on Friday apologised for "worsening social law and order" and said his government would take full responsibility.
